goal.name: Sleep quality
goal.definition: Composite of circadian alignment (melatonin phase / DLMO), sleep continuity (onset latency), sleep architecture (slow-wave and REM proportion), and subjective sleep quality (PSQI/ISI).

behaviors.name: Evening blue/short-wavelength light exposure (screens/devices)
behaviors.dose_or_intensity: ~2 h pre-sleep device use, unfiltered vs blue-blocked

behaviors.name: Caffeine consumption timing relative to bedtime
behaviors.dose_or_intensity: typical dietary doses (~100-220 mg), variable timing pre-bed

behaviors.name: Evening exercise (acute, by intensity)
behaviors.dose_or_intensity: low/moderate/high intensity, performed in the evening before bed

behaviors.name: Alcohol consumption before bed
behaviors.dose_or_intensity: low dose <=0.50 g/kg (~2 drinks) vs high dose >=0.85 g/kg (~5 drinks)

behaviors.name: Regular/acute exercise (general, not timing-specific)
behaviors.dose_or_intensity: varies across 66 pooled studies; not moderated by intensity per meta-analysis

markers.name: Melatonin phase (DLMO) / melatonin secretion
markers.unit: hours phase shift, or melatonin level

markers.name: Deep sleep (SWS) / REM sleep share
markers.unit: minutes or % of total sleep time

markers.name: Subjective sleep quality (PSQI / ISI)
markers.unit: PSQI or ISI score (points, lower = better)

edges.effect: 0.5-h morning bright light produced a phase advance of 1.8 +/- 0.8 h vs 2.4 +/- 0.8 h for 2-h light exposure (75% of the full 2-h effect)
edges.effect_normalized: ~1.8 h phase advance (75% of maximal 2.4 h shift)
edges.normalization_method: raw hours (continuous outcome, single RCT; no SMD computed)
edges.population: healthy adults, n=50 (27 male), mean age 25.9 +/- 5.1 y
edges.conditional_on: Combined with afternoon 0.5 mg exogenous melatonin (dosed progressively earlier) and a gradually advancing sleep/dark schedule (1 h/day x 3 days). Light-only effect is not isolated in this design.

paper.title: Phase advancing human circadian rhythms with morning bright light, afternoon melatonin, and gradually shifted sleep: can we reduce morning bright-light duration?

edges.verbatim: Compared to the 2-h group (phase shift = 2.4 +/- 0.8 h), smaller phase-advance shifts were seen in the 1-h (1.7 +/- 0.7 h) and 0.5-h (1.8 +/- 0.8 h) groups... the single 30-min bright-light exposure was as effective as 1 h of bright light spread over 3.25 h, and it produced 75% of the phase shift observed with 2 h of bright light.
edges.caveats: Confounded with concurrent melatonin administration and an advancing sleep schedule; cannot isolate light-only contribution. Small n=50, healthy young adults with normal sleep, not a clinical DSPD population.

edges.effect: Overnight melatonin secretion significantly higher (p<0.05) after wearing a blue-light shield than control eyewear during 2 h of pre-sleep device use, i.e. unfiltered blue light suppressed melatonin
edges.effect_normalized: directional only; no effect size reported (small crossover trial)
edges.population: 12 healthy adults using self-luminous portable devices 2 h before sleep
edges.conditional_on: Effect inferred from blocking blue light (proxy for blue-light exposure being harmful). Contradicted in a larger, more recent RCT in male schoolchildren (n=39) where blue-light-blocking glasses advanced sleep phase and improved behavior but did NOT alter salivary melatonin.

paper.title: Protective effect of blue-light shield eyewear for adults against light pollution from self-luminous devices used at night

edges.verbatim: Overnight melatonin secretion was significantly higher after using the blue-light shield (P < 0.05) than with the control eyewear. Sleep efficacy and sleep latency were significantly superior for wearers of the blue-light shield (P < 0.05 for both).
edges.caveats: Very small n=12, no effect size reported. Directly contradicted by a 2025 PLOS One RCT (DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0332877, n=39 schoolchildren): 'While blue light blocking glasses did not influence salivary melatonin levels, they significantly advanced the sleep phase' -- suggesting the sleep-phase benefit of blocking blue light may not always run through melatonin secretion.

edges.effect: Interventions reducing evening blue-light exposure improved PSQI with a large combined effect size: Hedge's g = -1.25 (95% CI -2.39 to -0.11)
edges.population: mixed healthy adults/adolescents and clinical populations (insomnia, major depressive disorder, delayed sleep phase syndrome, ADHD, bipolar disorder) across 12 pooled studies, 6-21 participants each
edges.conditional_on: PSQI result drawn from only the subset of the 12 included studies that reported PSQI; objective measures (sleep efficiency g=0.31, total sleep time g=0.32) showed only small-to-medium effects in the same review, so the large PSQI effect may partly reflect subjective/expectation bias rather than physiological change alone.

paper.title: Interventions to reduce short-wavelength ("blue") light exposure at night and their effects on sleep: A systematic review and meta-analysis
paper.design: systematic review and meta-analysis, 12 studies (8 RCT + 4 before-after)

edges.verbatim: large magnitude combined effects size (Hedge's g = -1.25; 95% CI: -2.39, -0.11)
edges.caveats: Wide confidence interval (crosses near zero at one bound), small per-study samples, heterogeneous designs and populations (healthy + clinical mixed).

edges.effect: Caffeine consumption increased sleep onset latency by 9 minutes on average
edges.normalization_method: pooled mean difference across included studies
edges.population: healthy adults, variable caffeine doses (e.g. 107 mg coffee, 217.5 mg pre-workout) and timings, 24 pooled studies
edges.conditional_on: In this pooled model the SOL increase was NOT significantly moderated by the amount or timing of the final caffeine dose; a separate dose-response model from the same research group estimated coffee should be consumed >=8.8 h and pre-workout supplements >=13.2 h before a 10pm bedtime to avoid reductions in total sleep time.

paper.title: The effect of caffeine on subsequent sleep: A systematic review and meta-analysis

edges.verbatim: Caffeine consumption reduced total sleep time by 45 min and sleep efficiency by 7%, with an increase in sleep onset latency of 9 min and wake after sleep onset of 12 min.
edges.caveats: Heterogeneous doses/timings pooled into one estimate. Deep sleep (N3/N4) duration also fell by 11.4 min and light sleep rose, so the 9-min SOL change is only part of a broader architecture shift.

edges.effect: Low-intensity evening exercise showed the greatest tendency (best rank) to shorten sleep onset latency vs no exercise in a network meta-analysis; no intensity significantly disrupted sleep overall
edges.effect_normalized: not quantified as a pooled point estimate in the abstract; ranking-based (SUCRA-style) network meta-analysis result
edges.normalization_method: n/a (ranking/network meta-analysis, no single SMD reported)
edges.population: healthy adults with good sleep, 28 pooled studies, n=325
edges.conditional_on: Intensity-dependent: low-intensity exercise best for shortening SOL; moderate-intensity best for WASO/sleep efficiency/SWS; high-intensity within 1 h of bedtime reduced REM sleep instead. Findings apply to healthy good sleepers, not clinical insomnia populations.

paper.title: Different Intensities of Evening Exercise on Sleep in Healthy Adults: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis
paper.design: systematic review and network meta-analysis, 28 studies

edges.verbatim: low-intensity exercise displayed the greatest tendency to shorten sleep onset latency... regardless of intensity, acute evening exercise completed before bedtime does not disrupt subsequent sleep in healthy young and middle-aged adults.
edges.caveats: No numeric SOL point estimate available in the abstract (network meta-analysis ranking only); studied only in healthy good sleepers.

edges.effect: Melatonin reduced sleep onset latency by 7.06 minutes vs placebo
edges.population: adults and children with primary sleep disorders (predominantly insomnia, some delayed sleep phase syndrome and REM sleep behavior disorder), 19 studies, n=1683
edges.conditional_on: This headline WMD averages across insomnia and delayed sleep phase syndrome subgroups; other dose-response meta-analyses in the same literature report the effect on SOL is generally larger in delayed-phase/circadian populations than in general insomnia, and peaks near a 4 mg/day dose -- this pooled paper does not itself break out that subgroup split numerically.

paper.title: Meta-Analysis: Melatonin for the Treatment of Primary Sleep Disorders
paper.design: meta-analysis of randomized, placebo-controlled trials, 19 studies

edges.verbatim: Subjects randomly assigned to melatonin fell asleep 7 minutes earlier on average than subjects receiving placebo (weighted mean difference (WMD) = 7.06 minutes [95% CI: 4.37 to 9.75])
edges.caveats: Absolute effect is modest (~7 minutes) despite melatonin's popularity as a sleep aid; total sleep time effect was similarly modest (WMD = 8.25 min).

edges.effect: Sleep onset latency and latency to deep sleep (N3) reduced, but ONLY at high alcohol dose (>=0.85 g/kg, ~5 standard drinks)
edges.effect_normalized: dose-threshold effect; not pooled as a single SMD in the abstract
edges.population: healthy adults aged 18-70y, controlled experimental alcohol-dosing studies, 27 pooled studies
edges.conditional_on: High dose only (>=0.85 g/kg). At low-to-moderate doses no significant SOL-shortening effect was established. This SOL-shortening at high dose co-occurs with, and likely drives, worse subsequent REM sleep disruption (see e8).

paper.title: The effect of alcohol on subsequent sleep in healthy adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis

edges.verbatim: Reductions in sleep onset latency and latency to deep sleep (i.e., non-rapid eye movement stage three (N3)) were only observed following the consumption of a high dose of alcohol (>=0.85 g kg-1 or approximately five standard drinks)... It appears that high doses of alcohol may shorten sleep onset latency, however this likely exacerbates subsequent REM sleep disruption.
edges.caveats: Effects on total sleep time, sleep efficiency, and wake-after-sleep-onset were too uncertain to pool (large heterogeneity) in this review, even though qualitative literature widely reports second-half-of-night fragmentation.

edges.effect: REM sleep onset delayed and REM duration reduced, occurring even at LOW alcohol dose (<=0.50 g/kg, ~2 standard drinks), worsening progressively with higher doses
edges.effect_normalized: dose-response gradient; no single pooled SMD reported in the abstract
edges.conditional_on: Occurs at LOW dose, unlike the SOL-shortening effect which requires HIGH dose -- this is the key subjective/objective dissociation: a couple of drinks can make falling asleep feel unchanged or easier while already suppressing REM.

paper.title: The effect of alcohol on subsequent sleep in healthy adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis

edges.verbatim: Changes in sleep architecture were observed, including a delay in the onset of rapid eye movement (REM) sleep and a reduction in the duration of REM sleep. A dose-response relationship was identified such that disruptions to REM sleep occurred following consumption of a low dose of alcohol (<=0.50 g.kg-1 or approximately two standard drinks) and progressively worsened with increasing doses of alcohol.
edges.caveats: This is a distinct, separately-dosed effect from e7 (SOL) -- recorded as its own edge per the alcohol subjective/objective dissociation, not averaged together.

edges.effect: Acute exercise: small beneficial effect on slow-wave sleep, small effect on REM sleep. Regular exercise: moderate beneficial effect on overall sleep quality.
edges.effect_normalized: qualitative Cohen's-scale categories as reported (small / small-to-medium / moderate); exact numeric g not given in the abstract
edges.normalization_method: SMD (categorical description only; precise value not extractable from abstract)
edges.population: mixed healthy and clinical adult samples, 66 pooled studies through May 2013
edges.conditional_on: Moderated by sex, age, baseline physical-activity level, exercise type, time of day, duration, and adherence. NOT significantly moderated by exercise intensity or aerobic/anaerobic classification.

paper.title: The effects of physical activity on sleep: a meta-analytic review

edges.verbatim: Analyses reveal that acute exercise has small beneficial effects on total sleep time, sleep onset latency, sleep efficiency, stage 1 sleep, and slow wave sleep, a moderate beneficial effect on wake time after sleep onset, and a small effect on rapid eye movement sleep.
edges.caveats: The publicly retrievable abstract reports only qualitative effect-size labels (small/moderate), not the exact numeric g values from the paper's tables -- flagged rather than estimated, per the no-assertion-from-memory rule.

edges.effect: PSQI total score reduced by 3.13 points vs control; large standardized effect
edges.population: adults >18y with a diagnosed insomnia disorder, 31 pooled RCTs, n=2449 (1107 intervention / 1342 control)
edges.conditional_on: Face-to-face delivered CBT-I specifically. Digital/internet-delivered CBT-I shows somewhat smaller but still large effects in other meta-analyses (SMD roughly -0.71 to -0.85 on insomnia severity).

paper.title: Efficacy of Face-to-Face Delivered Cognitive Behavioral Therapy in Improving Health Status of Patients With Insomnia: A Meta-Analysis
paper.design: meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials, 31 studies

edges.verbatim: significant improvement in sleep quality measured by Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index in the intervention group (mean difference = -3.13, 95% CI -3.71 to -2.56, p < 0.001, I2 = 0.00) in comparison with the control group, with large effect size (SMD = -0.96, 95% CI -1.25 to -0.68, p < 0.001)
edges.caveats: Low heterogeneity (I2=0.00) supports robustness. This is the largest effect size in the entire dataset -- the intended contrast with supplement-based interventions.

edges.effect: ISI score reduced by 3.9 points (magnesium) vs 2.3 points (placebo) from baseline to week 4; borderline significant, small effect
edges.population: healthy adults 18-65y with self-reported poor sleep quality for >4 weeks, n=153 (77 magnesium / 76 placebo), 250 mg elemental magnesium bisglycinate/day
edges.conditional_on: Measured via Insomnia Severity Index (ISI), not PSQI directly, mapped here to the PSQI/subjective-sleep-quality marker as the closest available self-report outcome. Exploratory subgroup analysis suggested a larger benefit in participants with lower baseline dietary magnesium intake, but this was hypothesis-generating only, not a pre-registered confirmed subgroup effect.

paper.title: Magnesium Bisglycinate Supplementation in Healthy Adults Reporting Poor Sleep: A Randomized, Placebo-Controlled Trial

edges.verbatim: The magnesium bisglycinate group showed a significantly greater reduction in ISI scores compared to the placebo group from baseline to Week 4 (-3.9 [95% CI: -5.8 to -2.0] vs -2.3 [95% CI: -4.1 to -0.4], respectively; p = 0.049). The effect size was small (Cohen's d = 0.2)
edges.caveats: This is the newest and best-powered magnesium RCT identified, yet the result is only borderline significant (p=0.049) with a small effect size. A prior systematic review of 5 magnesium RCTs for sleep found 2 of 5 showed NO improvement over placebo, with most studies rated low-to-fair quality and small sample sizes. Overall RCT evidence for magnesium and sleep quality should be read as a weak, unsettled signal -- not an established effect -- which is why it is retained here rather than dropped: this weak-but-real signal is itself the finding.

cut_edges.candidate: Ambient room temperature -> Sleep onset latency
cut_edges.reason: Could not obtain a verbatim, numerically-quantified result sentence from a resolvable-DOI primary source directly linking ambient/bedroom temperature to sleep onset latency in minutes. The one systematic review located with a clean DOI (Bennett et al. 2024, Sleep Medicine Reviews, DOI 10.1016/j.smrv.2024.101915, 'A systematic review of ambient heat and sleep in a warming climate') confirms only a directional association ('higher outdoor or indoor temperatures are generally associated with degraded sleep quality and quantity') with no minute-level quantification in its abstract. Other specific numeric claims surfaced during search (e.g. '5C increase -> ~2 min SOL increase', '+0.04 min per degF from 3.75 million nights') traced only to secondary AI-generated summaries or an unpublished conference abstract (SLEEP supplement) without a verifiable, resolvable-DOI verbatim sentence backing the exact number. Per the no-assertion-from-memory rule, this edge is cut rather than shipped with an unverifiable number.
